power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Digital health technology (DHT) is increasingly being integrated into healthcare delivery; however, limited research exists exploring the pre-acceptability of DHT among ageing respiratory patients.
This study aimed to identify the factors influencing the pre-acceptability of digital health technology in individuals with chronic respiratory disease in Ireland.
A quantitative study was conducted among respiratory service users attending two respiratory centres in the Midlands and West of Ireland.

A convenience-based questionnaire was developed and distributed, which was informed by prior Phase 1 qualitative findings that adopted the Technology Acceptance Model and the Health Belief Model.Data were analysed using non-parametric statistical methods, including the Mann-Whitney U test, to explore differences between gender and geographical location (urban/rural).
Fifty-eight participants completed the study.

Overall, participants demonstrated positive perceptions toward the use of DHT, particularly regarding support for self-management, hospital admission avoidance, increased symptom awareness, and enhanced engagement with healthcare professionals.
Perceived usefulness emerged as a significant factor influencing acceptability.
Concerns regarding privacy, data security, and digital literacy were less significant than anticipated.
Statistical differences were identified between urban and rural participants in relation to perceived usefulness, technology design preferences, feedback.
The global healthcare sector has witnessed accelerating interest in digital technologies to support and enhance clinical service delivery.
The COVID-19 pandemic served as a catalyst, rapidly exposing both the potential and necessity of remote healthcare solutions.

Digital health, encompassing e-health, m-health, and telehealth, offers opportunities to strengthen clinical engagement through advanced monitoring capabilities aimed at improving patient outcomes [1].

text.text: These technologies enable healthcare professionals to make more informed clinical decisions and elevate care quality, predicated on the assumption that service users possess both the capability and willingness to engage with such innovations.

Consequently, digital health technologies (DHT) represent a promising paradigm for symptom monitoring, treatment adherence support, and enhanced healthcare access across diverse patient populations [2].

text.text: The clinical evaluation schedule for this patient cohort, typically involving assessments at six-to-twelve-month intervals, may contribute to under-recognition of disease progression.
While increasing consultation frequency could address this gap, practical constraints including cost, time, and geographical accessibility often limit healthcare access.
Digital health technologies offer a potential solution by facilitating remote symptom self-management and ongoing monitoring.
Müller et al. [4] established that successful DHT utilisation is intrinsically linked to internet access and digital competence.

text.text: These authors observed higher DHT adoption rates among younger, more educated, and higher-income populations, suggesting that effective engagement requires concurrent health literacy and information technology proficiency.
Supporting this perspective, Neter and Brainin [5] documented that individuals with limited e-health literacy demonstrate reduced capacity to utilise available online health resources.

text.text: These conflicting perspectives underscore a critical research question: "What factors influence successful DHT adoption among ageing populations?"
Clinical investigations have examined DHT applications across various healthcare contexts.
Steel et al. [8] evaluated remote patient monitoring for asthmatic patients aged 17-50, reporting mean compliance of 80%.

During the study period, 48% received medical intervention, suggesting remote monitoring's potential to reduce asthma morbidity.

text.text: While numerous studies have evaluated purpose-designed devices for chronic diseases, highlighting age, gender, and physiological measurement influences, the specific factors affecting service user engagement or disengagement remain unclear from existing research.
Global DHT adoption patterns reveal significant variation, with wearable technologies lagging considerably behind established technologies such as smartphones and tablets [10].

text.text: The literature reveals considerable definitional variability regarding technology acceptance.

Perski and Short [14] conceptualised acceptability as an individual's attitude or willingness to engage with novel therapies or digital devices, encompassing pre-engagement willingness, actual usage, and post-engagement satisfaction.

text.text: While postusage evaluation may assess effectiveness, it fails to illuminate factors necessary for sustained engagement.
As healthcare continues its digital evolution, understanding service user perceptions becomes imperative.
This study therefore aims to identify and describe the factors influencing DHT preacceptability among respiratory patients as a specific end-user population.

text.text: The use of validated frameworks in conjunction with the data collected from phase 1 enhanced the rigor of the questionnaire, and ultimately resulted in a study that was well-founded.
External persons from the study were acquired for face and validity testing who reviewed the developed questionnaire independently.
The participants for the second phase of the study were recruited in two different Institutions by means of purposeful sampling.
A cohort of respiratory patients attending Portiuncula University Hospital and Galway University Hospital were recruited from 02/02/2022 to 13/04/2022.
They were invited to complete a questionnaire.
Written information was provided to each participant; consent was obtained and assurance that their decision not to participate would not have any impact on the care provided at that clinic.
Participants in this study were women and men resident in Ireland.
Inclusion criteria included service users with known respiratory disease attending respiratory services in the midlands/west of Ireland, English-speaking, and ≥60 years of age.
Exclusion criteria included non-English speaking individuals and those on active palliative pathways.
Ethical approval is important for all types of research.
This is to ensure the protection of participants, the researcher and the organisation they represent.
It aims to minimise the risk of harm to all involved.
Participants were provided written information in the form of a handout about the study, its pros and cons along with the benefits of participating in the study.
Ethical approval was first sought from the Technological University of the Shannon Research Ethics Committee, and upon gaining approval then ethical permission was sought from clinical sites.
Applications for ethical approval contained a copy of detailed information sheets and consent forms which was also attached for consideration.
The completed submissions were made on 12th December 2021 and approval was granted on January 15th, 2022.
The researcher carried out data collection from March 2022 to May 2022 (Ethical approval number C.A.2734).
The average number of patients attending both clinics over a 10-week period was estimated to be 300.
The assumption was of an average non-attendance rate of 15% [21] and an overall expected completion rate of 33% [22], with the estimated sample size for this study being 84.

text.text: The duration of this study was dictated by the secondment period agreed for the researcher and the permission of access to clinics by management in the HSE.
Participants could choose to complete the questionnaire at the time of the clinic or return via a supplied stamped addressed envelope provided.
Data was collected in the form of a questionnaire utilising a Likert Scale, which is ordinal data and cannot be considered normally distributed as the values are bound on the left and right.

To confirm that data were indeed not distributed normally, the researcher conducted a Shapiro Wilk Test, which did further confirm with a significance of .000 across both variables that the data was not normally distributed; therefore, for the purpose of this study non-parametric tests were considered for statistical analysis.
The non-parametric test selected was the Mann-Whitney U Test.
This study was conducted over a ten-week period collecting data from two separate institutions in the Midland and West of Ireland, with fifty-eight (58) individuals participating.
Of the fiftyeight participants, 44.8% (n=26) were male and 53.4% (n=32) were female.
The mean average of those who disclosed their age was 69.5.
Geographically, 32.8% (n=19) self-reported to be from an urban area and 55.2% (n=32) from a rural location.
In respect to technology skills, 52% (n=30) claimed to have self-taught skills, with no prior formal education.
Over 300 questionnaires were distributed with only 58 respondents, despite the provision of stamped addressed envelopes.

The key themes yielded from this study were: • Support of self-management of respiratory disease; • Engagement with healthcare professionals; • Design and ability of the technology to provide data feedback; • Security; • Digital literacy; • Perceived usefulness and awareness of digital health technology.

When participants were asked whether DHT would assist them in managing their respiratory disease, 26.5% (n=13) strongly agreed and 32.6% (n=16) agreed, while 32.6% (n=16) were unsure and 4% (n=2) disagreed.
Regarding hospital admission avoidance, 18.5% (n=10) strongly agreed and 37% (n=20) agreed that DHT would help reduce admissions, with 38.2% (n=21) uncertain and 5.5% (n=3) in disagreement.

Concerning feelings of security between healthcare appointments, 8.4% (n=4) strongly agreed and 46.9% (n=23) agreed that DHT would increase their sense of security, while 34.6% (n=17) were unsure and 10.2% (n=5) disagreed.
Notably, 17.3% (n=9) strongly agreed and 38.4% (n=20) agreed that DHT would empower them to take control of their chronic disease, with 40.8% (n=21) uncertain and 17.3% (n=9) disagreeing.

Mann-Whitney U tests comparing male versus female and urban versus rural perspectives revealed no statistically significant differences across any self-management or admission avoidance variables (all p > 0.05).

text.text: When asked whether they derived more value from face-to-face appointments, 33.3% (n=18) strongly agreed and 37% (n=20) agreed, with 14.8% (n=8) uncertain and an equal proportion disagreeing.
Regarding whether DHT would reduce required clinic appointments, 12% (n=6) strongly agreed and 48% (n=24) agreed, while 34% (n=17) were unsure and 6% (n=3) disagreed.

Interestingly, 9.5% (n=4) strongly agreed and 40.4% (n=17) agreed that they would prefer a reduction in appointments, with 26.1% (n=11) uncertain and 23.8% (n=10) disagreeing.Finally, when asked if DHT would increase overall contact with healthcare providers, 10.8% (n=5) strongly agreed, 39.1% (n=18) agreed, 39.1% (n=18) were unsure, and 10.8% (n=5) disagreed.
Mann-Whitney U tests demonstrated no significant differences between genders regarding any engagement variable (all p > 0.05).
text.formatted: Mann-Whitney U tests demonstrated no significant differences between genders regarding any engagement variable (all p > 0.05).

text.text: Similarly, no significant differences emerged between urban and rural participants regarding value placed on face-toface clinics or perceived increased contact with healthcare professionals (p = 0.60 and p = 0.81, respectively).
However, a statistically significant difference was observed between urban and rural cohorts regarding preference for reduction in face-to-face clinics (p = 0.01).
Rural participants demonstrated less preference for reduced clinic attendance compared to their urban counterparts.

Regarding technology size as a factor influencing adoption, 8.5% (n=4) strongly agreed and 36.1% (n=17) agreed that size would affect their decision, while 36.1% (n=17) were unsure and 19.1% (n=9) disagreed.
Visual acuity was considered important by 4.3% (n=2) who strongly agreed and 47.8% (n=22) who agreed, with 17.39% (n=8) uncertain and 30.4% (n=14) disagreeing.

Notably, 37.2% (n=19) strongly agreed and 50.9% (n=26) agreed that they would prefer the device to have the capability to provide health data feedback, with 11.7% (n=6) uncertain and no participants disagreeing.Mann-Whitney U tests revealed no significant differences between males and females regarding technology size, design features, or feedback capabilities (p > 0.05).

text.text: Conversely, statistically significant differences emerged between urban and rural participants regarding design features (p = 0.01) and the ability to provide health information feedback (p = 0.01).
Rural participants demonstrated less favourable attitudes toward DHT design features and expressed less interest in feedback capabilities compared to urban participants.
No significant difference was observed regarding the impact of technology size (p = 0.08).
When asked whether DHT would invade their privacy, 7.3% (n=3) strongly agreed, 29.2% (n=12) were unsure, and 63.4% (n=26) disagreed.
Regarding concerns about who would have access to their health data, 14.6% (n=6) strongly agreed, 21.9% (n=9) agreed, 21.9% (n=9) were unsure, and 41.4% (n=17) disagreed.
Concerning technology security, 17.02% (n=8) strongly agreed, 10.6% (n=5) agreed, 31.9% (n=15) were unsure, and 40.02% (n=19) disagreed.
Mann-Whitney U tests confirmed no statistically significant differences across gender or geographical variables (p > 0.05).

text.text: When asked to consider the statement "I do not have the IT skills to use technology," 17.6% (n=9) strongly disagreed and 41.1% (n=21) disagreed, while 15.6% (n=8) strongly agreed, 9.8% (n=5) agreed, and 15.6% (n=8) were unsure.
Mann-Whitney U tests revealed no significant differences between genders (p = 0.43) or geographical locations (p = 0.46).

When presented with the statement "Digital health technology is something that I feel would be useful to me," 18.8% (n=10) strongly agreed, 49% (n=26) agreed, 30% (n=16) were unsure, and 1.8% (n=1) disagreed.
Mann-Whitney U tests demonstrated no significant difference between male and female perspectives (p = 0.52).
However, a statistically significant difference emerged between urban and rural cohorts (p = 0.04), with rural participants expressing fewer positive perceptions of DHT usefulness.

When asked to consider the statement "I have never heard of digital health technology prior to participating in this study," 23.9% (n=11) strongly agreed, 30.4% (n=14) agreed, 30.4% (n=14) disagreed, and 15.2% (n=7) were unsure.
Mann-Whitney U tests confirmed no significant differences between genders (p = 0.47) or geographical cohorts (p = 0.23).
Perceived usefulness is one of the most important factors discussed in the literature when discussing acceptability and DHT.
People's understanding of why they are using DHT and what benefits it has for them significantly influences adoption.

This is evident in studies such as Shinoda et al. [10] whose research shows that wearable technology is accepted when it facilitates goal setting, provides reminders with useful feedback, and has the ability to share data with HCPs.

text.text: In this study, most participants strongly agreed or agreed that DHT would be useful to them.
Statistically, males and females' perspectives do not differ (p=0.528); however, there is an evident statistical difference between urban and rural cohorts (p=0.048).
There is a lack of clarity as to why there is a statistical difference between those from rural and urban areas.
One possible reason is simply a lack of awareness.
As previously discussed, the literature shows no evidence of exploration of the awareness of DHT.
This study found that 54.3% of participants had never heard of DHT prior to the study.
While there was no statistical difference between males and females or urban and rural areas, it is most definitely a concern.
There is an expectation or even worse, an assumption by those developing technology and HCPs that service users will engage with DHT.
Service users need to understand clearly why they need to use DHT and what benefits it will have for them.
Future research into the perspectives of urban and rural geographical location is required to gain a deeper understanding.

Those involved in the development of DHT, policy makers and clinicians need to be aware that there is a statistical difference, and remain cautious if assuming what works for urban areas will work for rural areas.

Digital health literacy is the ability to find, understand, and appraise health information from electronic sources and apply the knowledge gained to address or solve health problems [5].

text.text: This study aimed to address this gap by exploring preferences regarding technology design and capabilities.

Results showed that 44.6% agreed that technology size would influence their decision, 52.1% agreed visual acuity was important, and an overwhelming 88.1% agreed they would prefer the device to have the ability to feedback their health data.
It is clear that design and functionality are important contributing factors to the pre-acceptability of DHT.
Statistically, there are differences between the variables evaluated.

While males and females share similar perspectives, there appears to be a statistical difference between urban and rural areas regarding design features (p=0.018) and the ability to provide health information feedback (p=0.016).
It is imperative this difference is noted and taken into consideration during the design phase of DHT.
There is an urgency both at National and International level to develop policy documents in retrospect of the introduction of DHT.
Findings from this study will advance Digital Health Strategies in Ireland and Europe.
While digital health policies are in their infancy, successive National policies have used limited retrospective enquiry from patient perspective.

From an overarching system or national policy perspective, this use of bottom-up patient perspective will provide critical insight into understanding and eventual compliance with important new policies.Indicative outputs from this study indicate the following factors may be considered to inform key performance indicators: reliability, ease of use, numbers of patients supported expressing satisfaction, reduction in negative health outcomes, numbers up-taking new technology, cost savings to healthcare, adoption by healthcare service providers transregionally and internationally, policies informed, and adoption into education and training.
To date there are no KPIs identified for the measurement of DHT, ultimately there are no measurements of risk.
This study highlights multiple areas requiring future research.
Firstly, there is an apparent difference in perspectives of people from urban and rural geographical locations.
There is a lack of clarity on the reasoning behind these differences, which needs further investigation.
It is imperative that technology design is founded on research findings indicative of what service users want.
There will be potential exclusion of cohorts if these differences are not addressed.
Risk measurement and risk assessment are to the fore of any healthcare intervention; however, there is a heightened awareness when referencing DHT.
None of the studies in the scoping review referred to risk.
There were no quantifiable measures of risk identified nor explanation of protective strategies embedded in the study protocols.
There is an urgency both at National and International level to develop such documents.
Finally, to date, there is no evidence of standardisation of digital health technology.
In healthcare, the introduction of a new medication is processed via a rigorous protocol supported by research data.
There is a significant lack of policy and protocol to standardise the use of DHT in Ireland at present.
This is most definitely an area in need of urgent investigation.
This study is novel and the first to explore the pre-acceptability of digital health technology in the ageing respiratory patient.
This study shows that there is overall a lack of awareness of digital health technology and as a result poor trust.
It is evident that respiratory patients are indeed very open minded and willing to embrace the use of DHT.
A majority felt that they have the skills to engage and seemed open minded.

There were some differences noted in the perspectives of those from urban and rural geographical locations, and the rationale for this is somewhat unclear.The results indicate strong viewpoints of service users' preferences for what they would like DHT to look like and what functionality they would like it to have.
There is a positive role for DHT in the management of chronic disease, and participants do believe its use has merit pending the design.
Service users would also need encouragement that DHT is not intended to replace the HCP but to complement a service.

The skills required to use the technology and the overall security of the data were less of a concern than anticipated for this cohort.It is hoped that the findings of this study will contribute to policy and KPI development for digital health technology on a national and international level.

If consideration is given to the factors that contribute to the pre-acceptability of DHT, then future technology and implementation into practice will be based on a foundation of fact, not assumption..
